job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Wei Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Everyone I talk to is made up for this study, so there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts around eight-thirty at a company in Hamilton that makes heating and cooling units for office buildings. I'm a graduate design engineer, so I model parts like fan housings and brackets in CAD, run a few stress checks, and send the drawings to the shop floor. Around noon I walk out to the workshop to see whether what I drew can actually be built. After work I'm usually at the gym or at my girlfriend Lin's place, since she's in the middle of a nursing degree and I cook for her.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did mechanical engineering at McMaster, finished with a good average, and my final project was a heat exchanger for a small greenhouse. I did one four-month co-op at a tool maker. My dad is a machinist and my older brother Jun works in a car parts plant, so I'm the one with a desk. I started in August, I share a flat with two guys, I owe about twelve thousand and I have around two months of costs in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right. My team uses an AI chat tool now and then to draft emails and look up standards, and it's useful but not magic. I'd tell friends it's a better search engine and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm okay. Heating units get built in a factory, there's a real product, and our drawings still get checked by people who've been on the floor for thirty years. The things I think about are boring: pay, rent, when I might get a raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and ask for a step up in about two years. I'd try to learn the thermal simulation software, since senior people mostly know that and I'd be more useful. I'd keep saving about three hundred a month, and I'd begin looking at a small place with Lin once she's earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I'd say settled. I don't need much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the rent and pay worries in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They stay the same, and I think that's fine. My pay is typical for a first job, so I can cover the flat and eat well. The loan takes about two hundred a month, and I'd be done with it by thirty-one if I don't change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this world that could still go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company. If office building orders dry up, they'd stop hiring and I'd be the new one. That's a normal business risk, and I'd just find another firm. It happened a bit in 2020.

say: AI is a **better search engine**, useful but not magic.
I'd tell friends it's fine and leave it there.
think: Heating units are built in a **real factory** and checked by people with thirty years on the floor.
My worries are boring ones: **pay, rent** and a raise.
do: Ask for a **step up** in about two years.
Learn the **thermal simulation** software that senior engineers use.
Save **three hundred** a month and look at a small place with Lin.
feel: **Settled**, and I don't need much more than that.
S0.quote: If office building orders dry up, they'd stop hiring and I'd be the new one. That's a normal business risk, and I'd just find another firm.
fieldNote: Calm is **justified**: a physical product, a steady wage and a clear loan end date.
His fear is a normal **business cycle**, not AI.

steps.text: Ask for promotion to design engineer in two years
Save 300 pounds a month towards a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when you find out who adapts. At work I'd mention that parts of our job, like drafting drawings and checking tolerances, could be done by software. To friends I'd say learn the tools or someone will teach you them the hard way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little uneasy but not shaken. A chunk of my drawing work could shrink, and the company might hire one junior where it would have hired two. On the other hand, I'm a mechanical engineer, and the heavy, awkward, physical part of the job is slow to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI design tools more seriously, and I'd ask to do some time in the workshop, since the shop knows what real parts do. I'd also take a project management course online, because someone has to run the projects, and I'm decent with people. And I'd keep my cushion at about three months of costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert. A little excited, actually, because I like solving problems. But I'd be watching the pay line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the workshop that you couldn't do from a desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see how parts go wrong, like a bracket cracking because the weld's in the wrong place. A tool can draw a perfect bracket, but it won't know the welder hates that angle. That sort of knowledge is slow to get, and I'd be getting it while others are at their desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why project management specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the person who talks to the customer and keeps the job on schedule is harder to swap out than the one who draws. And my brother Jun says the best people at his plant aren't the cleverest, they're the ones who can get twelve people to agree.

say: This is when you find out **who adapts**.
I'd tell friends to learn the tools **first**, before someone makes them.
think: Drawing and tolerance checks could **shrink**, and the firm may hire one junior instead of two.
The heavy, awkward **physical** side of mechanical work is slow to change.
do: Spend time in the **workshop** to learn how parts go wrong.
feel: **Alert** and a little excited, while watching the pay line.
S1.quote: A tool can draw a perfect bracket, but it won't know the welder hates that angle.
fieldNote: Looks for the **tacit knowledge** AI lacks, in the workshop.
Draws on his brother Jun's view that **people skills** win.
Mood stays calm because his own role has hands-on parts.

steps.text: Use an AI design assistant for first-draft brackets and housings
Spend one day a week in the workshop with the welders
Keep three months of costs in the bank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big one and nobody can know exactly. At work I'd say let's see what the owners plan. Online I'd say governments should work with companies on a safety net, since people can't plan in two years. I'd be careful not to sound like I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is at risk. Design is thinking work, and if AI does it better and cheaper in 2028, the company needs maybe a third of the engineers. My workshop experience would help a bit, but only until about 2031 when robots do the physical work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut my spending, drop the gym fees and stop the takeaway habit. I'd focus on the part of the job that touches the real world, like commissioning and servicing the units, because installs and repairs will take longer to automate. I'd also talk to my dad about work as a machinist's apprentice for a spell, though I know that's not forever. And I'd keep Lin and me in a sensible plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stressed. I'd sleep badly for a month, and then I'd get on with a plan, because that's what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell Lin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Lin, I might lose my job within a couple of years, and I'd rather you heard it from me. She's training to be a nurse, so she's got a job that'll last, and she'd say, we'll work it out. That helps more than any plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the apprentice idea serious?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a back door. My dad has contacts, and a machine shop is hands-on, so I'd have three or four years of work before robots catch up. I'd hate it for a while, but it beats having no income.

say: It's **a big one**, and nobody can know exactly.
Governments and firms should work on a **safety net** because two years is short.
think: Design is thinking work, and the company may need **a third** of the engineers.
Workshop experience helps only until about **2031**, when robots do physical work.
do: Cut spending: drop the **gym** and the takeaway habit.
Move toward **commissioning and servicing** the units.
Ask my dad about a **machine shop** job as a back door.
feel: **Stressed** for a month, then I'd get on with a plan.
S2.quote: I'd say, Lin, I might lose my job within a couple of years, and I'd rather you heard it from me.
fieldNote: Careful not to **overclaim**; he says nobody can know exactly.
The machine-shop idea is a **back door** he doesn't love.
His girlfriend Lin, a nursing student, is his steady point.

steps.text: Drop the gym membership and takeaway nights
Ask to move into commissioning and servicing the heating units
Ask my dad about machine shop work through his contacts
Build savings to four months of costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something to plan for without freaking out. At work I'd ask the managers to be open about what they see coming. To friends I'd say get good at something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but hopeful. I'd have time to get a few years of experience and build something that isn't just drawing. The risk is that by 2031 firms wouldn't need me, and I'd be a 27-year-old with a loan and a lot of CAD.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim to become a registered professional engineer within four years, since that means my signature legally matters. I'd save about a quarter of my pay. I'd also do my best to move toward customers and project leads, and then keep a possible plan to start a small service company for maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Not scared, not relaxed. I'd feel I was doing the right things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of service company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small one that looks after offices. Heating units in mid-size buildings break down, someone has to go and fix them, and that's hands-on. I'd start it with my brother Jun, if his plant doesn't keep him. It's more of a lifeboat than a dream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pick between the engineering licence and the service company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The licence first, because it costs time but not money and it keeps both doors open. The company would only start when I saw the signs, like the firm cutting designers. I'd rather have the option than make the jump now.

say: Five years is something to **plan for** without freaking out.
I'd ask managers to be **open** about what they see coming.
think: I'd be uneasy but **hopeful**, with time to build more than drawing skills.
By 2031 the firm might not need me, leaving a **27-year-old** with a loan.
do: Become a **registered professional engineer** within four years.
Save about a **quarter** of my pay.
Move toward **customers** and project lead work.
feel: **Mixed**, not scared and not relaxed, feeling I'm doing the right things.
S3.quote: Heating units in mid-size buildings break down, someone has to go and fix them, and that's hands-on.
fieldNote: Prefers **options** to jumps: licence first, company only on signs.
Brother Jun is a possible **partner** in the service idea.
Realistic: he calls the service company a **lifeboat**, not a dream.

steps.text: Apply for professional engineer registration within four years
Save a quarter of each pay cheque
Plan a maintenance service company with my brother Jun
Move to a customer-facing project role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and it's the best case of the three. At work I'd say let's plan a proper career path, and to friends I'd say don't panic but don't be lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty good. I'd be 32, probably with a flat and maybe a kid on the way, and I'd have had ten years to stay useful. If AI gets there by 2036, I'd already be in a hands-on or customer side of the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job, get promoted to senior, and buy a flat with Lin once she's a nurse. We'd probably get married in about three years. I'd also keep adding skills that aren't pure design, like simulation and site work. And I'd put a decent chunk into an index fund each month, something I haven't done yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, with a bit of excitement. Like I've got a decent map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother Jun about this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him his plant has more time than he thinks, but to learn the machines, because the person who looks after the robots has a job. He'd say I'm over-thinking, and then he'd sign up for a night class anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any worry you'd still carry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan, until thirty-one. And the fact that ten years can sound long and be short. I'd check my progress against a list each birthday, and I'm a bit of a list person.

say: Ten years is a long time, and it's the **best case** of the three.
I'd tell friends **don't panic**, but don't be lazy.
think: I'd feel **pretty good**, maybe with a flat and a kid on the way.
By 2036 I'd already be in the **hands-on or customer** side of the business.
do: Get promoted to **senior** and buy a flat with Lin.
Plan a **wedding** in about three years.
Put a chunk into an **index fund** each month.
feel: **Settled**, with some excitement, like I've got a decent map.
S4.quote: I'd check my progress against a list each birthday, and I'm a bit of a list person.
fieldNote: Time produces a **practical life plan** with marriage and a flat.
Wants to bring his brother along: the person who looks after the **robots** has a job.
Self-description as a list person is consistent across the interview.

steps.text: Work towards senior design engineer within five years
Start an index fund with 150 pounds a month
Plan a wedding with Lin for about three years ahead
Save a flat deposit with Lin once she starts nursing

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Nobody, not me, not the company, not the government, would have time to do much. What would help is quick retraining that I don't have to pay for, a firm that tells people the truth, and some form of income support if I get let go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just this. People think engineers will be fine. The ones who'll be fine are the ones who stay curious and keep a hands-on skill. I'd like to be that person, and I plan to be.

headlineQuote: People think engineers will be fine. The ones who'll be fine are the ones who stay curious and keep a hands-on skill.
portrait: Wei Young is **22**, a graduate design engineer at a heating and cooling maker in Hamilton.
He did mechanical engineering at McMaster, owes about **twelve thousand**, and shares a flat while dating a nursing student.
He's a centrist and steady: he uses **AI now and then**, and adopts a tool once it has proven itself.
His mood runs from calm to **anxious** in the two-year world, where a machine shop job is his back door.
He plays the long game with a **licence**, project work and maybe a service company with his brother.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, since no one would have time to **prepare**.
whatWouldHelp: Free quick **retraining**, honest employers and income support if he's let go.
